posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-scoring compliance pain post with three ICP prospects engaging — validate the 'explainability' problem as the real blocker, not AI itself, to position credibility without pitching
posts.draft_comment: The ban isn't really about ChatGPT — it's about auditability. 'The model said so' is never going to fly in a regulated environment when someone's licence is on the line. The funny thing is, most teams aren't even asking for AI to do less, they just want to be able to trace the logic back to something they can defend in a room. That gap between 'here's the answer' and 'here's how we got there' is where trust dies.

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO frustrated with Power BI adoption failure — validate the pain precisely, then reframe the real problem as trust not tooling
posts.draft_comment: The 18 months wasn't wasted on the wrong tool — it was spent on the wrong problem. People don't quote numbers in board meetings because they don't trust where they came from, and no dashboard fixes that on its own. The trust gets built in the moments before the meeting, when someone can actually explain why the number is what it is. Did your finance team ever feel like they owned the data, or did it always feel like something IT handed them?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging on dashboard overload — validate the 47-KPI pain, add the 'who decides what stays' insight without pitching
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is basically no KPIs — everyone's covered but nobody's accountable. The cut from 47 to 5 is the easy part in hindsight, but in the room it's always a fight about whose metric gets dropped. What made the difference for you — was it a top-down call or did the team actually agree on what mattered?

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail) engaging with a post that nails the governance gap in self-service BI — validate the 'who owns truth' framing and add the insight that the tool is rarely the problem, the missing layer is shared definitions before the data even reaches the dashboard.
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports thing is so recognisable. The tool works exactly as advertised — it's just that nobody stopped to agree what 'revenue' meant before handing out licenses. Self-service BI doesn't fail because people can't build dashboards, it fails because the semantic layer gets skipped as if it's a boring admin task. Who in your org actually owns that problem — data team, finance, or does it just fall through the gap?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO framing hallucinations as a security risk (not just accuracy) with a CEO ICP prospect engaging — validate the reframe, add the trust layer insight, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The 'treat outputs like user inputs' framing is exactly right and I don't think most analytics teams have caught up to it yet. There's this assumption that because the AI is internal-facing the bar is lower — but a hallucinated revenue figure in a board deck can do as much damage as a data breach, just slower and quieter. Who's actually accountable when that number gets cited in an earnings call?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: CEO at 65-person firm calling out BI's self-service gap with a COO prospect engaging — validate the £200k horror story with a structural observation about who these tools are actually designed for
posts.draft_comment: That £200k story is painfully common. Most BI tools are designed to impress in a procurement meeting, not to survive contact with someone who just needs to answer a question before a client call. The 'self-service' label gets slapped on anything with a drag-and-drop interface, but that's not the same as a non-data person actually trusting what they're looking at. How much of that £200k do you think went on the tool vs. trying to make it work for people who never asked for it?

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a mid-market industrial company naming the real problem (culture, not tools) — validate the diagnosis and add the layer underneath it that most people miss
posts.draft_comment: Three teams, three filter configs, one awkward CFO moment — that's not a culture problem, that's a missing decision about who owns the number. Culture gets blamed when actually nobody ever sat in a room and said 'this is the single version, and these are the rules.' The AI conversation is a red herring. Has anyone in that business actually been made accountable for data definitions, or does that still fall between teams?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing the 'nobody knows what to ask' problem — validate the adoption gap insight and reframe it as a data literacy issue, not a tooling issue
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number is brutal but honestly not surprising. The gap isn't prompting skills — it's that most people don't have a clear enough mental model of their own data to know what question would even be useful to ask. Shadow AI on phones is just people finding the path of least resistance. What happens to adoption when the tool meets people where they are instead of waiting for them to get good at it?
